## ARIMA vs. ETS

Supposing that I'm an employee at a liquor store chain and I must forecast next month's U.S. sales to plan inventory, I've come up with some forecasting models and evaluated their accuracy against each other to determine the best model for predicting sales next month. The following sections compare the forecasting abilities of an ARIMA model, an ETS model, and their performance against the benchmark seasonal random walk (SNAIVE) model.

First, we'll load in the data: `MRTSSM4453USN`, which is retail sales at beer, wine, and liquor stores in the U.S., collected monthly and disseminated by FRED.

```{r}
#| echo: false

library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(BVAR)

liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))
```

Then, we'll plot `sales` and the natural log of `sales` in a season plot to get a sense of the trend and seasonal pattern.

```{r}
#| echo: false

liquor |> 
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly sales at beer, wine, and liquor stores",
    subtitle = "Data from U.S. Census Bureau's monthly retail trade survey, accessed via FRED",
    x = "Date (Month and year)", 
    y = "Retail sales, in millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()

liquor |> 
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly sales at beer, wine, and liquor stores",
    subtitle = "Data from U.S. Census Bureau's monthly retail trade survey, accessed via FRED",
    x = "Month", 
    y = "Logged retail sales (originally in millions of dollars)")
```

The level of `sales` is trending up over time. The data are also very clearly seasonal, where the month with the highest sales is December and the month with the lowest sales is January. The seasonal swings do grow with the level of the series, as seen in the plot of the data in levels (the first plot), which suggests that modeling a logged version of the data is worth it because logging evens out those swings across time in the series and allows us to see the real changes in the data better.

Next, we want to build forecasting models to try to predict what the series will look like next month. To do so, we'll be creating an ARIMA model and an ETS model, both using the log of `sales`. The specifications of the models will be determined by fitting both models over the entire sample period. The following code tells us what model specifications are chosen by `fable`.

```{r}
#| echo: false

liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```

For the ETS model, the chosen specification was ETS(A, A, A). This means that this model has an additive trend component, an additive seasonal component, and an additive error component. For the ARIMA model, the chosen specification was ARIMA(1, 0, 2)(2, 1, 1)\[12\] with drift. (I'm not sure what the "\[12\] w/ drift" part means.) These specifications tell us that the model contains 1 lag of our target variable, sales, 2 lags of the error term, 2 lags of the seasonal target variable, 1 lag of the seasonal error term, and that the model differenced the data seasonally one time.

Now that we've estimated the specifications of the models, we want to look a little more closely at the residuals of the ARIMA model to determine whether those residuals are white noise with some plots and a Ljung-Box test.

```{r}
#| echo: false

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()

liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6)
```

Based on the plots above, the residuals do mostly look like white noise! The bar plot shows them centered on zero, and they don't seem to be autocorrelated in the plot of the ACF. While there are some significant error terms, they don't seem to be connected to each other. The Ljung-Box test also resulted in a LB-stat of 120.39 and a p-value of approximately zero, so no statistically significant autocorrelation in the residuals of the ARIMA model were detected.

With an assurance that the ARIMA does not have autocorrelated residuals, we're free to move on to the horse race, where we'll compare the forecast accuracy of the ARIMA, ETS, and SNAIVE models against each other using their RMSE and MAE. We'll do so by running an expanding-window TS-CV where the first training sample includes 10 years of data. The code chunk below won't run the TS-CV, as that is very time-consuming, but it will pull up the saved results of the TS-CV when it was run the first time.

In this TS-CV, if my math is right, around 214 forecast origins will be considered? Or maybe it's 216 instead. Somewhere around there. I apologize for not having clear answer.

```{r}
#| echo: false

liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")

liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The date of the first forecast is January 2002, and the date of the last forecast is December 2019.

The model that forecasts the most accurately is the ARIMA model, with an RMSE of 81.93 and a MAE of 65.65. Both the RMSE and the MAE of the ARIMA model are less than the same accuracy metrics for the ETS and SNAIVE models, so both metrics agree that ARIMA is more accurate in forecasting `sales`.

However, without further testing, we can't say for sure that the ARIMA model's forecast accuracy being better than ETS or SNAIVE is statistically significant. So, we'll run ARIMA and ETS, then ARIMA and SNAIVE, through a Diebold-Mariano test with squared error loss to test for equal forecast accuracy.

```{r}
#| echo: false

liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)

liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)

```

When comparing the ARIMA model vs. the ETS model, the DM-stat was -2.9062, and the p-value was 0.004042. Since the p-value is less than 0.05 (and 0.01), we can reject the null hypothesis of the models having equal forecast accuracy at the 5% and 1% significance levels.

When comparing the ARIMA model vs. the SNAIVE model, the DM-stat was -10.755, and the p-value was less than 2.2e-16. With an even smaller p-value, it's clear that the two models do *not* have equal forecast accuracy at the 5% and 1% significance levels.

With all these calculations, we can conclude that the best model we can use among the ARIMA, ETS, and SNAIVE models to forecast next month's liquor store retail sales is the ARIMA model.

## Forecast Combination

However, we can't just choose ARIMA yet! Why, you may be asking? It's possible that by combining the point forecasts of our ARIMA and ETS models, we might get more accurate point forecasts overall... as long as one model isn't so much worse than the other. To find out whether combining the models is worth it for forecasting, we'll create an equal-weight combination of ARIMA and ETS.

```{r}
#| echo: false

liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

Compared to the models that go into it, `combo` is less accurate than ARIMA but more accurate than ETS. It's clear that ETS is inaccurate enough to make it worth dropping in the combination, leaving us again with the ARIMA model on its own.

Why might this be the case? Combining models is most helpful for creating more accurate point forecasts when the forecast errors of the models (in this case, ARIMA and ETS) aren't too similar to each other. What happens when we compute this correlation?

```{r}
#| echo: false

cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
```

Well, the correlation between the errors is pretty high. Since the difference in forecasting ability between ARIMA and ETS is significant (as determined in the previous section), and their forecast errors are highly correlated (correlation = 0.878), it makes sense that the combination of the two models did not beat ARIMA. Not only is ETS significantly worse than ARIMA, meaning that combining it with ARIMA would only create less accurate point forecasts, the errors are highly correlated, meaning that ETS is not making up for any of the forecast errors ARIMA already has and is only making them worse.

## VAR vs. BVAR

Switching our focus from forecasting liquor store retail sales, we now want to work with seasonally adjusted macroeconomic data — a lot of it. In doing so, we'll compare the forecast accuracy of two VAR models and two BVAR models.

Our data is taken from FRED-QD and contains 245 U.S. macroeconomic data series. We will be using a September 2026 vintage of the data specifically. We'll also only be using eight of the series from the data and turning them into measures quarterly of growth rates (between 1960 Q1 and 2019 Q4): GDPC1 (real GDP), PCECC96 (real consumption), GPDIC1 (real investment), PAYEMS (payroll employment), GDPCTPI (GDP price index), UNRATE (unemployment rate), FEDFUNDS (Federal Funds rate), and GS10 (10-year Treasury yield).

```{r}
#| echo: false

qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))

growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))

qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),     # real GDP
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),   # real consumption
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),    # real investment
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),    # payroll employment
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),   # GDP price index
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),     # unemployment rate
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),   # federal funds rate
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>    # 10-year Treasury yield
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

nrow(y)
head(y)

N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)
actual <- y[121:N, ]
```

The firs training sample for our TS-CV will include the first 120 quarters in the data, from 1960 Q1 to 1989 Q4. We'll then compare a VAR(1) model with a VAR(4) model where both models are forecasting each time series value one quarter ahead that is trained on this sample of the data. We will be producing 120 forecasts for each variable. The date of the first forecast is 1990 Q1, and the date of the last forecast is 2019 Q4.

The output of the code chunk below will be the RMSE of each variable for both models in order to compare their forecast accuracy. The top row is the RMSE numbers for the VAR(1) model and the bottom row is the numbers for the VAR(4) model.

```{r}
#| echo: false

var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)            # columns: y_t, then its lags 1 to p
  M <- ncol(z)                    # number of variables
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))   # constant, latest p lags
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}

rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))

rmse_by_var(fc_var1)
rmse_by_var(fc_var4)
```

Based on these metrics, it looks like the VAR(1) model forecasts better for each of the eight variable except the GDP price index, where there is only a very small difference between the VAR(1) and VAR(4). The smaller model probably forecasts better because it has fewer parameters and thus fewer chances to make estimation errors that drive up the RMSE.

Now, let's see if BVAR models can perform better than the VAR models. The following code chunk pulls up data from a previously-run TS-CV for BVAR(4) models using the Minnesota prior. One model has lambda = 0.3, and the other has lambda = 0.05 (meaning it shrinks the variable parameter estimates towards zero more aggressively than the model with the larger lambda).

We then compare the RMSE for each model and its variable estimates against each other—both of the VAR models and the BVAR models.

```{r}
#| echo: false

fc_bvar_03 <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_03.rds")

fc_bvar_005 <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_005.rds")

var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds") 

var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)

```

The BVAR(4) model when lambda = 0.3 forecasts better for all variables when compared to the VAR(4) model. What explains this difference is BVAR shrinking down the effects of each variable by biasing them towards zero, thus shaving away some of the estimation bias that may have come from fitting meaningless noise.

However, BVAR(4) is still less accurate overall than VAR(1), except for the real investment, GDP price index, and 10-year Treasury yield variables. While that might seem meaningful, the differences in the RMSE metrics for variables are quite small—the largest difference is in the real investment variable, so that difference might be statistically significant.

For the most part, shrinking the variables more aggressively in the BVAR(4) model created forecasts that were more accurate then the VAR(4) model, but the model with the lower lambda was actually less accurate that the model with the higher lambda *and* the VAR(1) model. (Specifically, the only variable that the lambda = 0.05 model forecast more accurately than the lambda = 0.3 model and VAR(1) model was the growth of the Federal Funds rate.) It seems that simply shrinking more aggressively does not create a more accurate model for these data. Though I don't know if I'd say that the winner's RMSE (the winner is probably the VAR(1) model) here would be a fair estimate of how accurately it will forecast in the future. We still haven't compared the VAR(1) model to any benchmark forecasting models, nor is it really clear with only this information whether these RMSE metrics are even competitive in the real forecasting world. There are many things we could still try out with these data (like an even looser prior than 0.3 for the BVAR model, or something other than the Minnesota prior, etc.) to determine the best forecasting model. Just going off of which RMSE is the smallest doesn't mean much in the grand scheme of things (also, we might get better results if we combine the point forecasts of multiple models—the possibilities are nearly endless).

Let's now test whether the VAR(4) and BVAR(4) with lambda = 0.3 are equally accurate with a Diebold-Mariano test in forecasting GDP growth and the unemployment rate. We want to get a sense of whether the shrinkage the BVAR(4) affords us makes statistically significant differences in forecast accuracy.

```{r}
#| echo: false

e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)
```

The difference in forecasting errors for GDP growth between VAR(4) and BVAR(4) when lambda = 0.3 is significant!

```{r}
#| echo: false

e_var4 <- actual[, "unrate"] - fc_var4[, 6]
e_bvar <- actual[, "unrate"] - fc_bvar_03[, 6]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)
```

However, the difference for unemployment rate growth between the two is NOT significant at the 5% or 1% significance level (it would be at the 10% significance level). This tells me that one model is not consistently better than the other, and that their errors might not be completely correlated. Since there were even more inconsistencies between other models, I'd want to check the statistical significance of each model's forecast accuracy differences. Additionally, it might not be a bad idea to try to combine the results of a few models and see if they can beat out VAR(1). With all this uncertainty, I'm even more confident that we can't immediately conclude that we should choose VAR(1) to forecast our macroeconomic data over all the other models.
